title: Fact-Check: Can Foreign Adversaries Really Hack US Voting Machines?
summary: In a stark assertion, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin declared that foreign adversaries "can change voter registration and your vote" through vulnerabilities in voting machines. "It's not even for debate," he said. But a closer look reveals a more nuanced reality. Computer scientist J. Alex Halderman, who has demonstrated voting machine hacks, confirms that hardware weaknesses exist. In a controlled experiment, he reprogrammed a machine to invisibly alter results. However, he emphasizes, "there's no evidence that voting machine vulnerabilities have ever been used to attack a real U.S. election." Real-world elections employ layers of defense: machines are stored in locked, video-monitored areas, kept offline, and tracked meticulously. A 2021 intelligence report found no foreign manipulation of votes in 2020. Most states now rely on hand-marked paper ballots, which provide a verifiable audit trail. Andrew Appel of Princeton notes that modern machines are more secure than those from 2000, though risks persist. Mullin's claim conflates theoretical possibility with practical reality. While experts agree that vigilance is crucial, the assertion that adversaries can definitively change votes lacks current evidence. The debate, it seems, is very much alive.
why_it_matters: Election security directly affects whether young people can trust that their future votes will count. Exaggerated claims can spread fear and lead to laws that make voting harder, while ignoring real software weaknesses could leave a door open for mischief. Finding the balance between alarm and evidence shapes democracy itself.

background_read: After the 2000 presidential election, when hanging chads and confusing punch‑card ballots in Florida caused a major recount, the U.S. poured money into modernising voting machines. Many jurisdictions replaced paper‑based systems with electronic machines, which research later showed could have security flaws.

J. Alex Halderman, a computer science professor at the University of Michigan, gained fame for demonstrating how some voting machines could be infected with malware that flips votes without leaving a trace. His work helped push states to return to paper ballots that can be audited by human eyes.

A 2021 report by U.S. intelligence agencies concluded that there was no evidence any foreign government changed votes in the 2020 election—though disinformation campaigns remain a concern. This assessment is often cited to push back against wide‑ranging hacking claims.

Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security Secretary, is a former congressman appointed by President Trump. His stark assertion contradicts the more cautious language of cybersecurity experts, who say vigilance is essential but that an actual undetected hack changing an election outcome has never been found.

INTELLIGENCE REVIEW: 2021 report found no foreign manipulation of 2020 votes
ANALYST VIEW: Andrew Appel—modern machines more secure, but risks remain
DEBATE STATUS: Mullin conflates theory with practice; experts say debate is alive

perspectives.description: From this viewpoint, sounding a loud alarm is a responsible way to keep election security on the national agenda. It pressures agencies to lock down every possible hole and may convince Congress to fund more upgrades.

Critics charge that Mullin’s sweeping statement misleads the public by ignoring real‑world protections. Such talk could fuel baseless conspiracy theories and cause some voters to lose faith in the system, even when no attack has succeeded.

Technologists have long known that any computer can be hacked in a lab. The gap between laboratory exploits and an operation that flips a national election is enormous, especially when machines are never online and paper ballots exist. Historically, most election‑tampering scandals have involved paper fraud, not cyberattacks.

The debate is pushing some states to mandate risk‑limiting audits and strengthen physical security. However, if dramatic, unsupported claims become normalised, lawmakers could use them to pass restrictive ID laws or even refuse to certify results. Training young voters to understand how their ballots are protected could be the best defence against disinformation.
